NS.1-1.label: Decimal Expansions
NS.1-1.example: 4/11 = 0.3636… repeats forever; √2 = 1.41421… never ends or repeats.

NS.1-2.label: Definitions & Examples
NS.1-2.example: Rational: a fraction of integers, like 3/4. Irrational: can't be, like √2.

NS.1-3.label: Classify by Decimal
NS.1-3.example: 0.375 stops and 0.333… repeats: rational. 0.1010010001… never repeats: irrational.

NS.1-6.label: Justify Classification
NS.1-6.example: 0.12112111211112… is irrational: it never ends and no block repeats.

NS.1-7.label: Sorting With Reasons
NS.1-7.example: −√25 = −5: integer, rational. √7: irrational, since 7 isn't a perfect square.

NS.1-8.label: Real Number Model
NS.1-8.example: Integers sit inside the rationals; irrationals sit beside them, since no number is both.

NS.1-9.label: Irrational Fractions
NS.1-9.example: 3π/4 is irrational: 3π is irrational, and dividing by 4 keeps it irrational.

NS.2-1.label: Non-Perfect Square Roots
NS.2-1.example: √20 is irrational because 20 is not a perfect square.

NS.2-3.label: Number Line Placement
NS.2-3.example: √14 ≈ 3.7, so plot it between 3 and 4, closer to 4.

NS.2-7.label: Placing Many Values
NS.2-7.example: √5 ≈ 2.24 goes between 2 and 3; π ≈ 3.14 is just left of √11 ≈ 3.32.

EE.1-1.label: Core Concepts
EE.1-1.example: In 6⁴, the base is 6 and the exponent is 4: 6 × 6 × 6 × 6.

EE.1-7.label: Error Analysis
EE.1-7.example: Wrong: (5³)⁴ = 5⁷. Fix: multiply the exponents, so (5³)⁴ = 5¹².

EE.2-3.label: Inverse Operations
EE.2-3.example: 14² = 196 and √196 = 14, so the square root undoes the square.

EE.2-4.label: Rational or Irrational Roots
EE.2-4.example: √169 = 13 is rational; √40 is irrational because 40 isn't a perfect square.

EE.2-8.label: Area & Volume
EE.2-8.example: A cube holds 27,000 in³: edge = ∛27,000 = 30 in, face = 30² = 900 in².

EE.3-8.label: Choosing Units
EE.3-8.example: 384,000,000 m = 3.84 × 10⁵ km; km fit long distances like Earth to Moon.

EE.3-9.label: Order of Magnitude
EE.3-9.example: 6 × 10³ vs. 3 × 10⁻⁶: exponents differ by 9, so about 10⁹ times (exactly 2 × 10⁹).

EE.4-4.label: One-Step Word Problems
EE.4-4.example: 4 × 10⁴ grains × 2.5 × 10⁻² g each = 1 × 10³ g of rice

EE.4-6.label: Multi-Step Problems
EE.4-6.example: (1.2 × 10⁸ L ÷ 1.5 × 10⁵ homes) × 30 days = 2.4 × 10⁴ L per home

EE.4-8.label: Reasonable Answers & Units
EE.4-8.example: (2.5 × 10³ m³)(1 × 10³ kg/m³) = 2.5 × 10⁶ kg, not 10⁹; that's 2,500 metric tons.

EE.7-1.label: One-Variable Equations
EE.7-1.example: 4x − 7 = 21: coefficient 4, constant −7; add 7, divide by 4: x = 7

EE.7-4.label: Three Solution Types
EE.7-4.example: Ends as x = 3: one solution; 0 = 6: no solution; 5 = 5: infinitely many.

EE.7-7.label: Inequalities
EE.7-7.example: 3(2 − x) + 5 ≤ 2x − 4 → x ≥ 3: closed dot at 3, shade right

EE.7-8.label: Justify Solution Types
EE.7-8.example: 2(3x − 4) + 5 = 6x − 3 gives −3 = −3, always true, so infinitely many solutions.

EE.7-9.label: Real-World Equations
EE.7-9.example: Lena 60 + 40w > Kai 150 + 25w → w > 6, so Lena has more starting week 7.

EE.8-1.label: What a Solution Means
EE.8-1.example: (2, −1) solves y = −2x + 3 and y = x − 3: it is on both lines.

EE.8-2.label: Solve by Graphing
EE.8-2.example: y = (1/2)x + 1 and y = −2x + 6 cross at (2, 2): solution (2, 2)

EE.8-3.label: Slopes & Intercepts
EE.8-3.example: y = 4x − 1 and y = 4x + 6: same slope, different y-intercepts → no solution

EE.8-4.label: Solve by Inspection
EE.8-4.example: x + y = 7 and x + y = 9: x + y can't equal both, so no solution.

EE.8-6.label: Justify Without Graphing
EE.8-6.example: y = 2x + 3 and 4x − 2y = −6 (also y = 2x + 3): same line, infinitely many

EE.8-8.label: Model & Interpret
EE.8-8.example: 2x + 300 = 8x → x = 50, y = 400: at 50 shirts, cost equals income ($400).

EE.8-9.label: Explain With Graphs
EE.8-9.example: y = 15x + 40 and y = 15x + 20 are parallel (same slope), never meet: no solution.
